===== 464a10a 02:24 Damià Vicens Ramis
frontend: show the real iPhone as x-ray line art, not a RoundedBox stack

The viewport drew a procedural handset: a few RoundedBoxes standing in for a
phone. That is fine scaffolding, but the whole premise of the project is that
the antenna is fighting *this* device's titanium frame, battery and shield
cans — and a generic slab shows none of it.

data/apple_iphone_15_pro/*.blend is now exported to
frontend/public/models/iphone15pro.glb (191 meshes, 5.4 MB, geometry only —
materials and normals stripped because the viewer draws edges, not surfaces).
Node names keep their __material suffix, so DeviceXray classifies each part
with no runtime lookup: 105 metal, 85 dielectric, 1 battery, 0 unresolved.

DeviceXray renders EdgesGeometry per part rather than shaded meshes. 191
nested solids shade into an opaque blob and the antenna lives inside them;
edges keep the interior legible, match how a mechanical drawing reads, and
give the app the same visual language as the offline renders
(placement_beauty_*.png, orbit_beauty.gif). Colour is the physics, not
decoration — the same conductor/dielectric split rf/placement.py makes at
1e4 S/m, with the battery called out because it is the classic antenna killer.
depthWrite is off so occluded edges show through: that is the x-ray.

The procedural handset stays as the Suspense fallback while the model streams.
An uploaded model still wins.

Verified without a browser: tsc clean, dev server serves the GLB (HTTP 200,
5409816 bytes, model/gltf-binary), page compiles 200 with no errors in the
Next log, and every node resolves to a material family.

===== 1c105f2 02:31 Damià Vicens Ramis
frontend: fix the model's axes and scale so markers land on the geometry

Two bugs, one visible symptom (pins floating off the phone):

1. The export used export_yup=True, converting Blender's Z-up to glTF's Y-up.
   That lays the handset on its side — measured on the old file: X=71.45
   (width), Y=10.96 (thickness), Z=146.60 (length) — while candidate pins and
   keep-outs stay upright in lib/geometry.ts's frame (x width, y length,
   z thickness). Re-exported with native axes: X=71.45, Y=146.60, Z=10.96.

2. DeviceXray scaled by (specHeight * SCALE / tallestAxis). That silently
   rescales the mesh whenever the spec's height and the model's disagree,
   sliding every marker off the part it should sit on. The export is already
   in millimetres on the same axes lib/geometry.ts uses, so the scale is
   SCALE itself; the model is centred at the origin, which is exactly where
   toScene() puts the device centre.

Verified numerically rather than by eye: model half-extents after centre+SCALE
are X±0.715 Y±1.466 Z±0.110 against markers at X±0.716 Y±1.476 Z±0.078 — 0.15 mm
out in width, 1.0 mm in length. The thickness gap (11.0 mm mesh vs 7.8 mm spec)
is the camera bump, which the real device has and the slab spec does not.

===== 8fa7ba8 02:49 Damià Vicens Ramis
frontend: never present a heuristic run as the agent's work

The orchestrator restarts a dead agent channel on the built-in heuristic so a
demo always ends with a result, and marks the run '<source>+mock-fallback'.
Sensible default, terrible thing to hide: with Devin returning 403 the UI
showed a finished run with 19 results and no hint that Devin never ran. A run
that looks like the agent's but isn't is worse than no run at all, and in
front of a judge it is fatal.

toSnapshot now carries agentFellBack, and AgentPanel shows an amber banner
saying Devin did not run, that the simulations below are real but the
reasoning that chose them is not Devin's, and to check the feed for the API
error. Verified live: agentFellBack=true on a run where Devin 403s.

Note for the team, not a code issue: the 403 is
'Your organization has a billing error. Error: out_of_quota'. Devin credit is
exhausted; top it up at app.devin.ai. The Mock/Devin switch in the Agent panel
already worked and still does - mock for fast iteration, Devin for the real
thing once quota is restored.

===== c41f9cf 02:58 Damià Vicens Ramis
agent: record one live Devin run, replay it forever

Devin costs quota and ~2.5 minutes per run, ~98% of which is the model
thinking. That is a bad fit for a demo you want to repeat, and impossible once
credit runs out - but MockAgent is not a substitute: it produces plausible
numbers with none of the reasoning, which is the part worth showing.

app/agent/replay.py wraps any agent through the same five-method AgentPort
seam, writes every turn to a tape, and plays it back. What comes back is
Devin's actual decisions and actual prose.

    AGENT=devin RECORD_TAPE=var/tapes/wifi24_devin.json  python scripts/dev_run.py
    AGENT=replay                                        python scripts/dev_run.py

Replay is strict about turn order and refuses a tape recorded for different
bands, rather than quietly serving decisions that do not describe this run -
that is the failure mode that makes recorded demos untrustworthy. The tape is
flushed after every turn, so a crash mid-run still leaves a usable prefix.

Committed tape: a real Devin fusion-mode run, 3 iterations, 41 solves, no
fallback. Verified byte-identical on replay in 1.3 s vs 2.5 min live - same
design (IFA at e_r2, 30.75 mm, 5 mm gap, S11 -16.1 dB, VSWR 1.37, 97.5%
efficiency), same rationale.

Also: DEVIN_MODE=fusion (Cognition's multi-model harness, frontier performance
at lower cost). 'turbo' is not a valid mode - the API accepts normal, fast,
lite, ultra, fusion, and rejects anything else with 422 before creating a
session, so the wrong value cost nothing.

UI now offers three agents: Mock (fast heuristic), Replay (recorded Devin,
free and instant), Devin (live). AgentKind had drifted into two definitions,
one with 'replay' and one without; unified on backend.ts.

===== a1c11e0 03:50 Damià Vicens Ramis
the solver now reads the real iPhone, and the UI stops explaining that it didn't

The viewer drew a 191-part iPhone while the solver read 'Handset A', a
generic 147.6 x 71.6 x 7.8 mm block with 9 components. That was not
cosmetic: every clearance number, every anchor and every 'nearest metal' the
agent reasoned about belonged to a phone nobody was looking at. The panel had
been made to confess it ('191 drawn parts, none of them meshed') - honest, but
explaining a defect instead of fixing it.

app/geometry/manifest.py adapts the committed blend_loader manifest into the
geometry dict classify() already reads. The two shapes differ only in derived
fields (size_mm, per-part extent_mm), so it is an adapter, not an importer,
and needs no bpy. default_spec() prefers it and falls back to the canned slab
when the manifest is absent.

Result: the agent now reads 'Apple iPhone 15 Pro: 176 components' - 103
conductors, 70 dielectrics, with real roles (frame, battery, display, shield,
ground). Same device the viewer draws, the placement screening screens, and
the offline renders render.

UI, from inspecting the rendered page rather than the source:
- Layer chips (Antennas/Keep-out/Labels) were saturated accent - three loud

  colour reserved for Run. Now quiet, and the accent means one thing.
- The spec editor sits in the transcript's scroll container, and the

Selftest green (7/7), dev_run green, tsc clean.

===== 42d2fdb 04:08 Damià Vicens Ramis
Report one verdict per candidate, and make the keep-out meetable

A GPS run said "all requirements met" beside "not all margins positive".
Both were reading the truth; they were reading different halves of it.

SimResult.meets_requirements covers S11 and efficiency only — the solver
measures electricals and has no opinion on geometry — but the UI rendered
it as the whole verdict. The winner sat 12.6 mm from a steel speaker under
a 14 mm keep-out and was announced as passing.

  report and the UI all carry the same verdict; meets_all combines them.
- The frontend names what actually passed instead of implying everything did.

===== 3080d01 04:35 Damià Vicens Ramis
Render this run's own evidence, and place antennas where the physics says

Five things that were each a version of the same defect: the screen
describing work the solver was not doing.

Evidence. rf/ could already draw the placement map, the x-ray, the S11 and
the field — but only for a demo run committed in the repo, which is a
picture of someone else's answer. A run now renders its own, for the device
actually loaded and the candidate actually chosen, after run_finished so it
can never gate the result. A checkbox beside the spec turns it on; a new
Evidence tab shows the strip and opens a <dialog> for the full view. MP4
carries the field clip (same frames as the GIF, a third of the bytes,
scrubbing for free). Served through a Next proxy: the browser never reaches
port 8000, and the traversal guard is on both sides.

The field animation had never actually run against a phone. Two bugs:
"coarse" is lambda/10 at f_high — 12 mm cells, wider than the phone is
thick, so the dump came back one cell deep — and the reader assumed
(3, nz, ny, nx) when openEMS handed back (3, nx, ny, nz). The axis order is
now recovered by matching axis lengths against the dump's own mesh instead
of assumed. Also: cmr10 is an OT1 TeX font whose 0x5F is a dot accent, so
every figure title rendered `c004_ifa_e_t1` as `c004˙ifa˙e˙t1`.

Placement. This is the one that mattered. make_anchors() walks the
perimeter of the bounding box on an 18 mm pitch — the same four corners for
any phone of the same outside size. So the positions on screen were generic,
which is the exact opposite of what this tool claims to do. Runs now take
their anchors from rf.placement.scan(): sweep the real internals, drop every
point that collides or crowds metal, rank what survives by escape fraction.
The best spot it returns, (31.5, 127.5) at 38% escape, is the same one the

It now renders `iphone15pro.glb` — 191 meshes exported from the .blend — as x-ray line art via `EdgesGeometry`, colored by the same conductor/dielectric split `rf/placement.py` uses. **Honesty fixes on the agent (02:49–02:58)** — the two most important for the demo:
- The orchestrator silently falls back to the built-in heuristic when the agent channel dies, and the UI showed that as a finished Devin run. Now there's an amber banner saying Devin didn't run.
- **Devin is out of quota**: 403 `out_of_quota`, billing error. Needs a top-up at app.devin.ai. That's your call to make.

Viewer drew 191 iPhone parts while the solver read "Handset A", the canned 9-component slab — the thing you committed at 01:25 (fe54672). New `app/geometry/manifest.py` adapts the blend manifest into the geometry dict `classify()` reads: the agent now sees 176 real components, 103 conductors.

**Physics calibration (04:08–05:16)** — several real defects:
- Keep-out ladder (24/14/12/9/7 mm) was written for the slab; against the real iPhone it left B5 with **0% legal volume** — every run was a rigged FAIL. Recalibrated to chip-antenna practice (6/5/4/3/2.5 mm), now 9.5–42% legal.

An autonomous agent (Devin) places antennas inside a real phone. It reads the
build file, proposes where each antenna goes and what type it is, a solver
scores every proposal against the band requirements, the evidence goes back,
and the agent iterates until the design is good enough — then writes the

**13.6 MB on disk. 291,127 lines** added in commit `a1c11e0` — where the actual engineering in that same commit is about **2,900 lines**. The real work is buried 100:1 under the sweep.

## Why it's there

It's the design skill Damià used to do the overnight UI work — and that work is exactly what the commits show: the x-ray viewer, the panel rewrites, the evidence gallery, the dock. It's a multi-tool installer, so it wrote itself into all four directories regardless of which one he uses.

Then `git add -A` picked it up. That it was unintended isn't a guess — he hit the identical accident twice more and cleaned both up, naming the cause each time: `4db9f61` *"Remove a verification agent's scratch file that git add -A swept in"* and `b769feb` *"Remove pitch-deck scratch scripts that git add -A swept in"*. He just never noticed the 597 in the earlier commit.

## Does it hurt anything

Not the product. I grepped `backend/ frontend/ rf/ tools/ scripts/ data/` — **nothing references it**. It's tooling for whoever's coding, not code that ships. Your app runs identically with or without it.

What it does cost:
- Repo weight, and it's in history now — a fresh clone pays the 13.6 MB whether or not you delete it today.
- `git log --stat` and any diff review is unreadable across that commit.
- Third-party `.mjs` with hook configs that auto-fire — if a judge clones this and opens it in Cursor or Codex, those hooks run. Low risk, but it's someone else's executable code sitting in your repo.

1. **Don't `rm -rf .agents/`.** `.agents/skills/blend-extract/` is *yours* — you added it in `9925435`, and it's the skill the Devin agent uses to extract `.blend` geometry. Only the `impeccable` subtree goes.

unreadable.

.github/skills, .gemini/skills and .cursor/skills are byte-identical copies of
each other, so they go wholesale. Under .agents/skills only impeccable goes —
blend-extract is ours, added in 9925435, and it is the skill the agent runs to
turn a .blend into geometry.

edit hooks, and .gemini/settings.json and .github/hooks/entire.json are pure
Entire. So the impeccable entries were lifted out of the two mixed files and
the Entire ones left exactly as they were — all 7 per file before and after,
both still valid JSON — rather than deleting the files.

Ignore rules follow the same split, so the next install cannot re-enter the
tree while blend-extract stays tracked.

History still carries the 13.6 MB; this only stops it growing and makes the
working tree honest about what the project is.
